title: Germany's Coal Commission reaches near-unanimous coal exit compromise
programme: Commission on Growth, Structural Change and Employment (Coal Commission)
problem: Conflict between utilities, unions, coal regions and environmental groups over the future of coal blocked a German coal exit plan.
solution: In June 2018 the federal government set up a 31-member commission of energy industry, coal regions, business, unions, environmental groups and scientists with a clear mandate. Ministries attended only as non-voting participants.
delivery_partners: Commission office at the Federal Ministry of Economics and Energy
Commission members from regions, industry, trade unions, environmental associations and science
results: Within six months the Commission produced a roadmap to end coal power by 2038, adopted in January 2019 by a 27:1 vote; Agora credits a consensus culture, a clear mandate, non-voting ministries and years of prior studies.
serbia_reason: Serbia needs a socially accepted lignite exit plan, and a structured commission of the utility, unions, mining municipalities and NGOs could build one. Germany shows that a clear mandate and non-voting ministries help reach agreement.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to adapt the model to a weaker tradition of consensus politics and include the state utility as a central party.
blockers: Low trust between government, unions and civil society may prevent a balanced commission from forming.
quote: Within six months, the Commission succeeded in drawing up a detailed proposal for phasing out coal-fired power generation. It was adopted almost unanimously at the end of January 2019.

title: Coal exit timetable with capacity caps and periodic reviews
problem: Germany was set to miss its climate targets, largely because of high emissions from coal power.
solution: The Commission proposed no new coal plants or mines, capping coal capacity in the market at 30 GW by 2022 and 17 GW by 2030, and closing the last plant by 2038 at the latest, with a 2032 check on a 2035 exit. Progress reviews are set for 2023, 2026 and 2029, and the Federal Network Agency can refuse closures that threaten system stability.
results: Agora's modelling finds the 2030 energy-sector target highly likely to be met if coal falls to 17 GW and renewables reach 65%, avoiding some one billion tonnes of CO2 by 2038; the compromise alone is not enough for Germany's overall 2030 target.
serbia_reason: A capacity-based timetable with review points could give Serbia a credible lignite exit path while protecting security of supply. The reviews allow the exit to be accelerated as conditions change.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need its own capacity milestones based on its lignite units and a regulator empowered to check supply security.
blockers: Serbia's high lignite share and limited replacement capacity make early milestones hard to set.
quote: The calculations conducted for this study indicate that it is highly probable that the climate target for the energy sector can be achieved in 2030 if coal-fired power plant capacity is reduced to 17 gigawatts by 2030 and renewable energy is raised to 65 per cent of gross electricity consumption.

title: Negotiated and auctioned compensation for early coal plant closures
programme: Coal Commission compensation for power plant operators
problem: Closing coal plants early required legal certainty and the agreement of plant operators.
solution: Lignite closures are to be agreed with operators in negotiated contracts that include compensation and are then fixed by law, while hard coal closures from 2023 to 2030 are decided by competitive bidding. If no deal is reached by 30 June 2020, the government is to impose a closure schedule with compensation.
results: Agora estimates compensation at 5 to 10 billion euros, limited by EU state aid law; critics argue the payments are not legally required, while Agora expects bidding to set hard coal compensation efficiently.
serbia_reason: Any Serbian payments linked to early closure of lignite units would fall under Energy Community state aid rules, which also limited German compensation. The mix of negotiation and auctions offers a template for setting amounts.
adapt_needed: Because Serbia's lignite plants are state-owned, compensation design would need to focus on worker and regional costs rather than operator profits.
blockers: Tight public finances and state aid scrutiny under the Energy Community Treaty could restrict compensation.
quote: On the basis of European state aid law, however, it can be assumed that compensation payments will only be made available to a limited extent, over a limited period of time, and are also degressive. In total, the compensation paid to all power plants is thus likely to be between 5 and 10 billion euros.

title: EUR 40 billion structural aid and federal jobs for coal regions
programme: Structural aid for coal regions (Coal Commission)
problem: Coal-mining regions faced the loss of value added and jobs as coal power is phased out.
solution: The Commission proposed funding for energy modernisation, faster planning, transport and digital infrastructure and local research, plus relocating federal government offices with 5,000 employees to coal regions by 2028.
funding: Federal budget, 40 billion euros over 20 years.
results: Agora judges the scale and long-term nature of the aid should enable sustainable development in the regions; the 40 billion euros is the largest item in an estimated 69 to 93 billion euros of extra federal costs to 2038.
serbia_reason: Kolubara and Kostolac will need long-term regional investment, not only payments to workers, to replace lignite jobs. Relocating public-sector jobs is a lever the Serbian government also controls.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to scale the package to its budget and rely more on EU and development-bank funding.
blockers: Serbia lacks Germany's fiscal capacity to fund regional aid on this scale.
quote: In the short and medium term, federal government offices with a total of 5,000 employees are to be located in the coal regions by 2028 at the latest. These measures are to be financed by an additional 40 billion euros over the next 20 years for the coal regions.

title: Early retirement and retraining guarantee for coal workers
programme: Labour market measures for coal workers (Coal Commission)
problem: Around 20,850 people worked directly in the lignite industry and faced job losses from the phase-out.
solution: Coal workers are to receive protection against dismissal, retraining and help moving to new jobs, and employees aged 58 and over get adjustment payments to retire early without financial loss.
results: Agora estimates the early-retirement measure at 5 to 7 billion euros and concludes the labour package will ensure no coal industry employee is left high and dry.
serbia_reason: Workers at Serbia's lignite mines and plants would need similar guarantees before accepting a phase-out. Bridging older workers to retirement reduces resistance and the number who need new jobs.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to fit early-retirement terms to its pension system and budget.
blockers: Pressure on the public pension fund and budget could limit generous early-retirement offers.
quote: For employees of the coal industry aged 58 and up, the goal is to enable early retirement without financial losses. This measure will cost 5 to 7 billion euros.

title: Continue CHP support to replace coal plants supplying district heat
problem: Coal CHP plants supplied 33.5 TWh of district heating in 2017, so closing them risked heat supply.
solution: The Commission recommends continuing the Combined Heat and Power Act until 2030 to promote replacing coal plants with CHP facilities, while moving support towards flexible CHP systems.
funding: Support payments under the Combined Heat and Power Act.
results: 113 of 145 coal units can co-generate heat; Agora's modelling assumes gas-fired CHP replaces coal heat, and continued CHP support is one of the safeguards for supply security during the exit.
serbia_reason: Many Serbian towns get district heat from coal or lignite-fired plants, so a lignite exit must plan replacement heat supply. Germany links coal closures to supported conversion of heat generation.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to steer conversion towards flexible, low-carbon heat sources rather than locking in gas.
blockers: Low regulated heat tariffs and indebted municipal heating companies limit investment in new CHP.
quote: In order to ensure a sufficient supply of heat energy, the Combined Heat and Power Act is to be continued until 2030 and, among other things, the replacement of coal-fired power plants with CHP facilities is to be promoted. At the same time, however, the government support system is to be further developed in the direction of flexible CHP systems.

title: Cancel EU ETS allowances freed by coal closures to avoid leakage
programme: Cancellation of EU ETS allowances (Coal Commission)
problem: Under the EU emissions trading system, national coal closures can free allowances that let emissions rise elsewhere (a waterbed effect).
solution: The Commission recommends that the federal government cancel the quantity of EU ETS allowances freed by the coal exit, and examine carbon pricing in sectors outside the ETS.
results: Agora estimates cancellation will cost 3 to 4 billion euros and finds that, with coal replaced mainly by domestic renewables, displacement of emissions abroad can be almost completely avoided.
serbia_reason: As Serbia aligns with EU carbon pricing and faces CBAM, its coal closures will interact with ETS rules in the same way. Germany shows how to make a national coal exit count inside the EU carbon market.
adapt_needed: Serbia would first need a carbon pricing system linked to the EU ETS before cancelling allowances becomes relevant.
blockers: Serbia has no emissions trading system yet, so this tool applies only after ETS alignment.
quote: Since the phase-out of coal-fired power generation is to be replaced primarily by domestic renewable energy and the CO 2 certificates that are freed up will be cancelled, the displacement of CO 2 emissions abroad can be almost completely avoided.

title: Paid lignite reserve fell far short of climate targets
programme: Lignite capacity reserve (Climate Protection 2020 Action Programme)
problem: Germany was heading to miss its 2020 climate target, and the economy ministry's proposed coal measures met intense opposition from plant operators and unions.
solution: As an alternative, the government created a capacity reserve that holds 2.7 GW of old lignite-fired plants out of the market, with generous payments to operators.
funding: Payments to plant operators; the source gives no amount.
results: The reserve was expected to deliver 11 to 12.5 million tonnes of extra CO2 abatement in 2020, but the measures adopted were far from enough; Germany expected only around a 32% emissions cut by 2020 against a 40% target.
serbia_reason: Shows that paying to idle a few old lignite units buys little climate progress at a high price. Serbia should not treat reserves as a substitute for an exit plan.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to use any reserve only as a temporary security-of-supply tool within a binding exit timetable.
blockers: Security-of-supply worries may push Serbia to keep old lignite units in costly reserves.
quote: On the one hand, the measures adopted were far from sufficient for ensuring compliance with the 2020 and 2030 climate protection targets.
